front: What is the most common reason for palliative radiation?
back: A painful bone metastasis
extra: Others: bleeding, obstruction, and neurologic compromise (cord compression, brain metastases).

front: Which cancers most often spread to bone?
back: Prostate, breast, lung, kidney, and thyroid (plus myeloma in the marrow)
extra: Axial skeleton and proximal long bones, where red marrow is.

front: Prostate cancer bone metastases are usually lytic or blastic?
back: Blastic (bone-forming)
extra: Kidney, thyroid, and myeloma are lytic; breast and lung are often mixed. Lytic lesions carry more fracture risk.

front: How long does pain relief take after palliative bone radiation?
back: It usually starts in 1-2 weeks and peaks at about 4-6 weeks
extra: So a patient with only days to live may not benefit.

front: What are the two ways low-dose radiation treats benign disease?
back: Anti-inflammatory (a few Gy, e.g. osteoarthritis) and anti-proliferative (moderate doses, e.g. Dupuytren, keloid, heterotopic ossification)
extra: Functional and vascular radiosurgery (trigeminal neuralgia, AVM) is a third, very high single-dose group.

front: Which patient factor most limits benign radiation, and why?
back: Young age, because the lifetime risk of a radiation-induced cancer is highest in young patients
extra: Also keep the thyroid, breast, eyes, and gonads out of the field.

front: In palliative care, what three things replace stage in deciding the plan?
back: The goal, the prognosis, and the stability of the bone or spine (and whether the cord is safe)
extra: Also ask about prior radiation to the same area.

front: What is the single most useful predictor of survival in a palliative patient?
back: Performance status (KPS or ECOG)
extra: Clinicians tend to overestimate survival, which leads to courses that are too long.

front: Why can a bone scan miss multiple myeloma?
back: Bone scan detects bone formation, and myeloma lesions are purely lytic
extra: Use a skeletal survey, low-dose CT, MRI, or PET instead.

front: What SINS score should prompt a spine surgery consultation?
back: 7 or higher
extra: 0-6 stable, 7-12 potentially unstable, 13-18 unstable. Radiation doesn't fix an unstable spine.

front: Mechanical vs biologic pain: which suggests spinal instability?
back: Mechanical pain (worse with movement or loading, relieved by lying still)
extra: Biologic pain (steady, worse at night, better with steroids) comes from the tumor and responds to RT.

front: What does a Bilsky grade 3 mean?
back: Epidural tumor compressing the cord with no CSF visible around it
extra: Grade 2: compressed cord with CSF still visible. Grades 2-3 are high grade.

front: In the NOMS framework, why does histology matter for a patient with high-grade cord compression?
back: Radiosensitive tumors (lymphoma, myeloma, breast, prostate) can get conventional RT even with high-grade compression; radioresistant tumors (kidney, melanoma, sarcoma) often need surgery first or SBRT.
extra: NOMS = Neurologic (Bilsky), Oncologic (radiosensitivity), Mechanical (SINS), Systemic (fitness and prognosis).

front: What Mirels score means high fracture risk and a referral for prophylactic fixation?
back: 9 or higher
extra: Four features scored 1-3: site, pain, lesion type, and fraction of the bone's width involved. 8 is borderline.

front: Which pain feature in a lytic femur lesion warns of impending fracture?
back: Pain with weight bearing (functional pain)
extra: Protect weight bearing and get orthopedics involved.

front: For an uncomplicated painful bone metastasis, how do 8 Gy in 1, 20 Gy in 5, and 30 Gy in 10 compare for pain relief?
back: Equal pain relief
extra: About 60% respond and about a quarter become pain free.

front: What is the trade-off of 8 Gy in 1 compared with 30 Gy in 10 for bone metastases?
back: About twice as much retreatment (about 20% vs 8%), for fewer visits and less acute toxicity
extra: RTOG 9714 (8 Gy in 1 vs 30 Gy in 10, breast and prostate) and the Dutch Bone Metastasis Study (8 Gy in 1 vs 24 Gy in 6).

front: For neuropathic bone pain (pain following a nerve root), which regimen is often preferred over 8 Gy in 1?
back: 20 Gy in 5
extra: TROG 96.05 couldn't prove 8 Gy in 1 was as good. Longer courses also fit long expected survival and post-fixation RT.

front: What reduces the risk of a pain flare after palliative bone RT?
back: Dexamethasone around treatment (NCIC SC.23)
extra: Pain flare occurs within the first few days in roughly a third of patients.

front: Can a bone metastasis be re-irradiated after 8 Gy in 1?
back: Yes; a second 8 Gy in 1 was noninferior to 20 Gy in 5 or 8 in the main analysis of NCIC SC.20
extra: With fewer side effects.

front: What did SC.24 show for painful spine metastases?
back: SBRT 24 Gy in 2 gave more complete pain responses than 20 Gy in 5
extra: RTOG 0631 found single-fraction SBRT (16-18 Gy) no better than 8 Gy in 1 for pain at 3 months.

front: What did the Gillespie trial show?
back: Prophylactic RT to asymptomatic high-risk bone metastases reduced skeletal-related events and hospitalizations and improved survival (randomized phase II)
extra: High risk: bulky (2 cm or more), hip, shoulder, or SI joint, junctional spine, or posterior vertebral involvement.

front: What did SABR-COMET show?
back: SABR to up to 5 metastases (controlled primary) plus standard care improved overall survival (randomized phase II)
extra: With a small risk of treatment-related death. NRG-BR002 showed no benefit in oligometastatic breast cancer.

front: What is oligoprogression?
back: Most disease is controlled on systemic therapy but a few sites are growing; treat those sites and stay on the drug
extra: CURB: SBRT for oligoprogressive NSCLC improved PFS, but not for breast cancer.

front: What is the palliative head and neck quad shot?
back: 3.7 Gy twice daily for 2 days (14.8 Gy in 4), repeated every 4 weeks up to 3 times
extra: Controls pain, bleeding, and fungating tumor with little toxicity.

front: Who gets radium-223, and what did ALSYMPCA show?
back: Castration-resistant prostate cancer with symptomatic bone metastases and no visceral metastases; it improved overall survival
extra: An alpha emitter that behaves like calcium. Strontium-89 and samarium-153 relieve pain only.

front: What are the first two orders for suspected metastatic spinal cord compression?
back: Dexamethasone and an MRI of the whole spine
extra: A common dexamethasone regimen is a 10 mg IV load, then 16 mg a day in divided doses.

front: What is the strongest predictor of walking after treatment for cord compression?
back: Whether the patient can walk before treatment
extra: Back pain often precedes weakness by weeks; bladder and bowel dysfunction are late signs.

front: What did the Patchell trial show?
back: Decompressive surgery followed by RT kept more patients walking, and for longer, than RT alone
extra: Selected patients: single-area compression, non-radiosensitive tumors, not paraplegic over 48 hours. 84% vs 57% ambulatory.

front: Can a patient with cord compression and a short prognosis be treated with a single fraction?
back: Yes; 8 Gy in 1 gave walking outcomes close to 20 Gy in 5 (SCORAD III)
extra: ICORG 05-03: 10 Gy in 1 noninferior to 20 Gy in 5. Longer courses may give better local control for longer survivors.

front: What is the most common cause of malignant SVC syndrome?
back: Lung cancer (especially small cell), then lymphoma
extra: Catheter-related thrombosis is a growing benign cause.

front: In a stable patient with SVC syndrome and no diagnosis, what comes before radiation?
back: A biopsy
extra: Small cell, lymphoma, and germ cell tumors get chemotherapy first, and RT before biopsy can ruin the pathology. A stent gives the fastest relief if symptoms are severe.

front: Which SVC syndrome findings make it a true emergency?
back: Stridor (laryngeal edema) or confusion (cerebral edema)
extra: Most patients have collaterals and are not in immediate danger.

front: After fixation of a pathologic long-bone fracture, what does postoperative RT cover?
back: The full length of the hardware
extra: Usually a multifraction course (20 Gy in 5 or 30 Gy in 10); improves function and lowers repeat surgery.

front: What dose range is used for painful osteoarthritis or plantar fasciitis?
back: About 0.5-1 Gy per fraction, 3-6 Gy total
extra: Dutch sham-controlled trials (Mahler) found no benefit over sham in knee and hand OA; Niewald found 6 Gy beat 0.6 Gy for heel pain.

front: Which patients with Dupuytren disease benefit from radiation?
back: Early disease: nodules and cords with little or no contracture
extra: Established contractures need needle aponeurotomy, collagenase, or surgery.

front: What is a typical radiation regimen for early Dupuytren disease?
back: About 30 Gy in two courses of 5 x 3 Gy, 6-12 weeks apart (or 21 Gy in 7)
extra: Orthovoltage or electrons with a 1-2 cm margin. The same approach treats Ledderhose disease.

front: What is the strongest risk factor for heterotopic ossification after hip replacement?
back: Prior heterotopic ossification
extra: Others: ankylosing spondylitis, DISH, hypertrophic osteoarthritis, male sex.

front: What radiation prevents heterotopic ossification, and when is it given?
back: A single 7-8 Gy within about 24 hours before or 72 hours after surgery
extra: Shield uncemented, porous prosthesis components. NSAIDs are the alternative.

front: When is radiation given for a keloid?
back: Within about 24-48 hours after excision
extra: Excision alone often fails. Recurrence is higher on the chest and shoulder than on the earlobe.

front: Why must gynecomastia radiation be given before antiandrogen therapy starts?
back: Once breast tissue has grown and become fibrotic, radiation works poorly
extra: A single low dose with electrons; tamoxifen prevents it even more effectively.

front: What is the classic presentation of trigeminal neuralgia?
back: Brief, electric shock-like, one-sided facial pain in V2 or V3, triggered by touch, chewing, or brushing teeth
extra: In a young patient or with bilateral symptoms, think of multiple sclerosis.

front: What is the first-line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia?
back: Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine)
extra: Procedures are for drug failure or intolerance.

front: What is the SRS dose for trigeminal neuralgia?
back: A maximum dose of about 70-90 Gy in one session to the trigeminal nerve root
extra: A single 4 mm shot a few millimeters in front of the pons; dose prescribed to the center, not the edge.

front: What is the main side effect of radiosurgery for trigeminal neuralgia?
back: Facial numbness or tingling
extra: Relief usually starts within 1-3 months; pain can recur over years and SRS can be repeated.

front: What three features make up the Spetzler-Martin AVM grade?
back: Size, eloquent location, and deep venous drainage
extra: Size under 3 cm 1, 3-6 cm 2, over 6 cm 3; eloquent 1; deep drainage 1. Small deep or eloquent AVMs are the classic SRS cases.

front: What is the typical marginal dose for AVM radiosurgery?
back: About 16-25 Gy in one session (often 18-22 Gy)
extra: Obliteration occurs in roughly 70-80% of small AVMs.

front: After AVM radiosurgery, when is the patient protected from bleeding?
back: Only after complete obliteration, which usually takes 1-3 years
extra: Confirm with angiography, usually around 3 years.

front: What did the ARUBA trial show?
back: For unruptured AVMs, medical management alone led to fewer strokes and deaths than intervention over its short follow-up
extra: Debated, but it made observation a real option for unruptured AVMs.

front: What dose of ISRT is used after short chemotherapy for favorable early Hodgkin lymphoma?
back: 20 Gy
extra: GHSG HD10 (favorable, 20 Gy) and HD11 (unfavorable, 30 Gy). PET-adapted trials allow omission in some patients.

front: What is the curative radiation dose for early-stage follicular lymphoma?
back: 24 Gy ISRT
extra: FORT: 24 Gy controlled disease better than 4 Gy in 2, which is used for palliation.

front: What is the first treatment for gastric MALT lymphoma?
back: H. pylori eradication
extra: RT (about 24-30 Gy) if it persists or is H. pylori negative.

front: Preoperative vs postoperative RT for extremity sarcoma: what is the trade-off?
back: Preoperative RT causes more wound complications; postoperative RT causes more permanent fibrosis, edema, and stiffness
extra: Same local control (NCIC SR2). Preoperative is now commonly preferred.

front: How is a solitary plasmacytoma treated?
back: Definitive RT, about 40-50 Gy
extra: Myeloma, in contrast, needs only low palliative doses.

front: For which skin cancer locations is radiation especially useful?
back: The nose, eyelid, lip, and ear
extra: Avoid on the lower leg, in young patients, and in radiation-sensitizing syndromes.

front: What is the main dose-limiting organ in total body irradiation?
back: The lungs (pneumonitis)
extra: Myeloablative TBI: about 12-13.2 Gy in 6-8 twice-daily fractions before allogeneic transplant.
